claim: HDAC3 is critical for the development of CD4 T cells.
source: We found that histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) is critical for the development of CD4 T cells, as HDAC3-deficient DP thymocytes generate only CD8SP thymocytes in mice.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding based on experimental observations in mice.

claim: HDAC3-deficient DP thymocytes generate only CD8SP thymocytes in mice.
source: We found that histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) is critical for the development of CD4 T cells, as HDAC3-deficient DP thymocytes generate only CD8SP thymocytes in mice.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation stated in the abstract.

claim: MHC Class II-restricted OT-II thymocytes are redirected to the CD8 cytotoxic lineage in the absence of HDAC3.
source: In the absence of HDAC3, MHC Class II-restricted OT-II thymocytes are redirected to the CD8 cytotoxic lineage, which occurs with accelerated kinetics.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from experimental data.

claim: Redirection of MHC Class II-restricted OT-II thymocytes to the CD8 lineage occurs with accelerated kinetics in the absence of HDAC3.
source: In the absence of HDAC3, MHC Class II-restricted OT-II thymocytes are redirected to the CD8 cytotoxic lineage, which occurs with accelerated kinetics.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this temporal characteristic of the redirection.

claim: HDAC3-deficient DP thymocytes are biased towards the CD8 lineage prior to positive selection.
source: Analysis of histone acetylation and RNA-seq reveals that HDAC3-deficient DP thymocytes are biased towards the CD8 lineage prior to positive selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by histone acetylation analysis and RNA-seq data as stated in the abstract.

claim: Commitment to the CD4 or CD8 lineage is determined by whether persistent TCR signaling or cytokine signaling predominates, respectively.
source: Commitment to the CD4 or CD8 lineage is determined by whether persistent TCR signaling or cytokine signaling predominates, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is consistent with the kinetic signaling model referenced in the introduction.

claim: HDAC3-deficient DP thymocytes exhibit elevated IL-21R/γc/STAT5 signaling.
source: Despite elevated IL-21R/γc/STAT5 signaling in HDAC3-deficient DP thymocytes, blocking IL-21R does not restore CD4 lineage commitment.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this observation from experimental data.

claim: Blocking IL-21R does not restore CD4 lineage commitment in HDAC3-deficient DP thymocytes.
source: Despite elevated IL-21R/γc/STAT5 signaling in HDAC3-deficient DP thymocytes, blocking IL-21R does not restore CD4 lineage commitment.
evidence: This is an explicit experimental finding stated in the abstract.

claim: HDAC3 binds directly to CD8-lineage promoting genes.
source: Instead, HDAC3 binds directly to CD8-lineage promoting genes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, likely from ChIP experiments.

claim: HDAC3 is required to restrain CD8-lineage genes in DP thymocytes for the generation of CD4 T cells.
source: Thus, HDAC3 is required to restrain CD8-lineage genes in DP thymocytes for the generation of CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing multiple experimental findings.

claim: CD8 T cells directly kill pathogen-infected cells.
source: T cells are essential components of the adaptive immune system that directly kill pathogen-infected cells (CD8 cytotoxic T cells) or orchestrate other immune cells in host defense (CD4 helper T cells).
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: CD4 T cells orchestrate other immune cells in host defense.
source: T cells are essential components of the adaptive immune system that directly kill pathogen-infected cells (CD8 cytotoxic T cells) or orchestrate other immune cells in host defense (CD4 helper T cells).
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: The decision to become either a CD8 or CD4 T cell occurs in the thymus.
source: The decision to become either a CD8 or CD4 T cell occurs in the thymus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T cell development stated in the introduction.

claim: After positive selection, thymocytes downregulate the CD8 coreceptor to become 'intermediate' CD4+CD8lo thymocytes to test for coreceptor specificity.
source: After positive selection, thymocytes downregulate the CD8 coreceptor to become 'intermediate' CD4+CD8lo thymocytes to test for coreceptor specificity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T cell lineage commitment referenced from the kinetic signaling model (Singer et al., 2008).

claim: MHC class II-restricted thymocytes experience persistent TCR signaling.
source: MHC class II-restricted thymocytes experience persistent TCR signaling, upregulate the CD4-lineage determining transcription factor ThPOK, and commit to the CD4 lineage.
evidence: This is part of the kinetic signaling model described in the introduction, citing Singer et al., 2008.

claim: MHC class II-restricted thymocytes upregulate the CD4-lineage determining transcription factor ThPOK.
source: MHC class II-restricted thymocytes experience persistent TCR signaling, upregulate the CD4-lineage determining transcription factor ThPOK, and commit to the CD4 lineage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD4 lineage commitment stated in the introduction.

claim: TCR signaling ceases with MHC class I-restricted thymocytes.
source: Alternatively, TCR signaling ceases with MHC class I-restricted thymocytes, allowing for common gamma chain cytokine signaling (mainly IL-7R) to predominate, induction of the CD8-lineage determining transcription factor Runx3, and commitment to the CD8-lineage.
evidence: This is part of the kinetic signaling model described in the introduction.

claim: Common gamma chain cytokine signaling (mainly IL-7R) predominates in MHC class I-restricted thymocytes after TCR signaling ceases.
source: Alternatively, TCR signaling ceases with MHC class I-restricted thymocytes, allowing for common gamma chain cytokine signaling (mainly IL-7R) to predominate, induction of the CD8-lineage determining transcription factor Runx3, and commitment to the CD8-lineage.
evidence: This is part of the kinetic signaling model described in the introduction.

claim: Runx3 is the CD8-lineage determining transcription factor.
source: Alternatively, TCR signaling ceases with MHC class I-restricted thymocytes, allowing for common gamma chain cytokine signaling (mainly IL-7R) to predominate, induction of the CD8-lineage determining transcription factor Runx3, and commitment to the CD8-lineage.
evidence: This is established knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: HDAC3 exists in a large (~270 kDa) multiprotein co-repressor complex containing the nuclear receptor corepressor (NCOR) and/or its homolog silencing mediator of retinoic and thyroid receptors (SMRT).
source: HDAC3 exists in a large (~270 kDa) multiprotein co-repressor complex containing the nuclear receptor corepressor (NCOR) and/or its homolog silencing mediator of retinoic and thyroid receptors (SMRT) (reviewed by Karagianni and Wong, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDAC3 structure cited from a review.

claim: HDAC3 can associate with p300 coactivator complexes to modulate histone acetyltransferase activity.
source: HDAC3 can also associate with p300 coactivator complexes (Zhang et al., 2016) to modulate histone acetyltransferase activity.
evidence: This is cited from Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: HDAC3 does not have a DNA-binding domain.
source: HDAC3 does not have a DNA-binding domain, therefore it must be recruited to different areas of the genome via interactions with different transcription factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDAC3 structure and function.

claim: HDAC3 must be recruited to different areas of the genome via interactions with different transcription factors.
source: HDAC3 does not have a DNA-binding domain, therefore it must be recruited to different areas of the genome via interactions with different transcription factors.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the lack of DNA-binding domain.

claim: HDAC3 can be found at promoters or enhancers within the nucleus.
source: Within the nucleus, HDAC3 can be found at promoters or enhancers and functions to deacetylate specific lysine residues on histones H3 and H4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDAC3 localization and function.

claim: HDAC3 functions to deacetylate specific lysine residues on histones H3 and H4.
source: Within the nucleus, HDAC3 can be found at promoters or enhancers and functions to deacetylate specific lysine residues on histones H3 and H4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDAC3 enzymatic function.

claim: Genomic deletion of HDAC3 is embryonically lethal due to defects in gastrulation.
source: Genomic deletion of HDAC3 is embryonically lethal due to defects in gastrulation (Montgomery et al., 2008), therefore conditional knockout models are necessary to elucidate HDAC3 function in particular cell types.
evidence: This is cited from Montgomery et al., 2008.

claim: HDAC3 is important for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells.
source: Within the immune system, HDAC3 is important for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (Summers et al., 2013), peripheral T cell maturation (Hsu et al., 2015), regulatory T cell development and function (Wang et al., 2015), iNKT cell development and differentiation (Thapa et al., 2017), B cell development (Stengel et al., 2017), and macrophage function (Mullican et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Summers et al., 2013.

claim: HDAC3 is important for peripheral T cell maturation.
source: Within the immune system, HDAC3 is important for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (Summers et al., 2013), peripheral T cell maturation (Hsu et al., 2015), regulatory T cell development and function (Wang et al., 2015), iNKT cell development and differentiation (Thapa et al., 2017), B cell development (Stengel et al., 2017), and macrophage function (Mullican et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Hsu et al., 2015.

claim: HDAC3 is important for regulatory T cell development and function.
source: Within the immune system, HDAC3 is important for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (Summers et al., 2013), peripheral T cell maturation (Hsu et al., 2015), regulatory T cell development and function (Wang et al., 2015), iNKT cell development and differentiation (Thapa et al., 2017), B cell development (Stengel et al., 2017), and macrophage function (Mullican et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Wang et al., 2015.

claim: HDAC3 is important for iNKT cell development and differentiation.
source: Within the immune system, HDAC3 is important for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (Summers et al., 2013), peripheral T cell maturation (Hsu et al., 2015), regulatory T cell development and function (Wang et al., 2015), iNKT cell development and differentiation (Thapa et al., 2017), B cell development (Stengel et al., 2017), and macrophage function (Mullican et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Thapa et al., 2017.

claim: HDAC3 is important for B cell development.
source: Within the immune system, HDAC3 is important for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (Summers et al., 2013), peripheral T cell maturation (Hsu et al., 2015), regulatory T cell development and function (Wang et al., 2015), iNKT cell development and differentiation (Thapa et al., 2017), B cell development (Stengel et al., 2017), and macrophage function (Mullican et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Stengel et al., 2017.

claim: HDAC3 is important for macrophage function.
source: Within the immune system, HDAC3 is important for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (Summers et al., 2013), peripheral T cell maturation (Hsu et al., 2015), regulatory T cell development and function (Wang et al., 2015), iNKT cell development and differentiation (Thapa et al., 2017), B cell development (Stengel et al., 2017), and macrophage function (Mullican et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Mullican et al., 2011.

claim: HDAC3 is required during thymocyte development for positive selection.
source: In addition, HDAC3 is required during thymocyte development for positive selection and CD4-lineage development (Philips et al., 2016; Stengel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Philips et al., 2016 and Stengel et al., 2015.

claim: HDAC3 is required during thymocyte development for CD4-lineage development.
source: In addition, HDAC3 is required during thymocyte development for positive selection and CD4-lineage development (Philips et al., 2016; Stengel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Philips et al., 2016 and Stengel et al., 2015.

claim: CD2-icre-mediated deletion of HDAC3 results in a positive selection block due to the failure to down-regulate RORγt.
source: Mice with CD2-icre-mediated deletion of loxP-flanked Hdac3 (CD2-icre HDAC3-cKO, referred to as HDAC3-cKO) exhibit a positive selection block due to the failure to down-regulate RORγt (Philips et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Philips et al., 2016.

claim: Deletion of RORγt and transgenic expression of Bcl-xl corrects the positive selection defect in HDAC3-cKO mice.
source: Deletion of RORγt and transgenic expression of Bcl-xl corrects the positive selection defect in HDAC3-cKO mice (RORγt-KO Bcl-xl Tg HDAC3-cKO, referred to as RB3), as RORγt-KO corrects for the failure to down-regulate RORγt and the Bcl-xl transgene restores the DP-survival defect in RORγt-KO mice (Philips et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Philips et al., 2016 and Sun et al., 2000.

claim: RB3 mice have thymocytes that almost exclusively develop into CD8SP with very few CD4SP.
source: However, thymocytes almost exclusively develop into CD8SP with very few CD4SP (Philips et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Philips et al., 2016.

claim: RORγt-KO Bcl-xl Tg mice exhibited normal numbers of CD4SP and CD8SP thymocytes.
source: RORγt-KO Bcl-xl Tg mice exhibited normal numbers of CD4SP and CD8SP thymocytes (Philips et al., 2016), demonstrating that the defect in CD4-lineage development in RB3 mice is specific to HDAC3.
evidence: This is cited from Philips et al., 2016.

claim: The defect in CD4-lineage development in RB3 mice is specific to HDAC3.
source: RORγt-KO Bcl-xl Tg mice exhibited normal numbers of CD4SP and CD8SP thymocytes (Philips et al., 2016), demonstrating that the defect in CD4-lineage development in RB3 mice is specific to HDAC3.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between RORγt-KO Bcl-xl Tg mice and RB3 mice.

claim: Mature SP thymocytes from OT-II mice were primarily CD4+ cells.
source: While mature SP thymocytes and splenic T cells from OT-II mice were primarily CD4+ cells, OT-II RB3 mice generated CD8+ cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: OT-II RB3 mice generated CD8+ cells instead of CD4+ cells.
source: While mature SP thymocytes and splenic T cells from OT-II mice were primarily CD4+ cells, OT-II RB3 mice generated CD8+ cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: Mature SP thymocytes from OT-II RB3 mice expressed Runx3 and lacked ThPOK expression.
source: In addition, mature SP thymocytes from OT-II RB3 mice expressed Runx3 and lacked ThPOK expression (Figure 1B), demonstrating that MHC class II-restricted thymocytes are re-directed to the CD8-lineage in OT-II RB3 mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and stated in the text.

claim: OT-II RORγt-KO Bcl-xl tg (OT-II RB) mice showed normal commitment to the CD4 lineage.
source: Control OT-II RORγt-KO Bcl-xl tg (OT-II RB) mice showed normal commitment to the CD4 lineage (Figure 1A–B), indicating that the redirection observed in OT-II RB3 mice is a result of HDAC3 deletion.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 1A-B and stated in the text.

claim: The redirection observed in OT-II RB3 mice is a result of HDAC3 deletion.
source: Control OT-II RORγt-KO Bcl-xl tg (OT-II RB) mice showed normal commitment to the CD4 lineage (Figure 1A–B), indicating that the redirection observed in OT-II RB3 mice is a result of HDAC3 deletion.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between OT-II RB and OT-II RB3 mice.

claim: Redirection to the CD8-lineage was not dependent on Bcl-xl expression.
source: Redirection was not dependent on Bcl-xl expression, as OT-II RORγt-KO HDAC3-cKO mice also showed redirection to the CD8-lineage compared to OT-II RORγt-KO mice (Figure 1C), despite a reduction in the number of SP thymocytes in RORγt-deficient mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and stated in the text.

claim: OT-II RORγt-KO HDAC3-cKO mice showed redirection to the CD8-lineage compared to OT-II RORγt-KO mice.
source: Redirection was not dependent on Bcl-xl expression, as OT-II RORγt-KO HDAC3-cKO mice also showed redirection to the CD8-lineage compared to OT-II RORγt-KO mice (Figure 1C), despite a reduction in the number of SP thymocytes in RORγt-deficient mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and stated in the text.

claim: OT-I cells produced Granzyme b and Perforin upon TCR stimulation.
source: As expected, OT-I cells produced Granzyme b and Perforin, while OT-II and OT-II RB cells did not (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and stated in the text.

claim: OT-II and OT-II RB cells did not produce Granzyme b and Perforin upon TCR stimulation.
source: As expected, OT-I cells produced Granzyme b and Perforin, while OT-II and OT-II RB cells did not (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and stated in the text.

claim: CD8SP cells from OT-II RB3 mice made Granzyme b and Perforin upon TCR stimulation.
source: However, CD8SP cells from OT-II RB3 mice made Granzyme b and Perforin upon TCR stimulation (Figure 1D), demonstrating that CD8-lineage cells from OT-II RB3 mice are functionally cytotoxic-lineage cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and stated in the text.

claim: CD8-lineage cells from OT-II RB3 mice are functionally cytotoxic-lineage cells.
source: However, CD8SP cells from OT-II RB3 mice made Granzyme b and Perforin upon TCR stimulation (Figure 1D), demonstrating that CD8-lineage cells from OT-II RB3 mice are functionally cytotoxic-lineage cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the production of Granzyme b and Perforin.

claim: OT-II thymocytes differentiated to the CD4-lineage in β2m-KO recipients.
source: Since the OT-II TCR is MHC class II-restricted, OT-II thymocytes differentiated to the CD4-lineage in β2m-KO recipients (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and stated in the text.

claim: OT-II RB3-expressing CD8SP cells developed in β2m-KO recipients.
source: In addition, thymocytes from OT-II RB3 mice also did not select off of MHC class I, as OT-II RB3-expressing CD8SP cells developed in β2m-KO recipients (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and stated in the text.

claim: CD8-lineage differentiation in OT-II RB3 mice is not due to aberrant selection off of MHC class I.
source: Therefore, CD8-lineage differentiation in OT-II RB3 mice is not due to aberrant selection off of MHC class I.
evidence: This is inferred from the bone marrow chimera experiments in β2m-KO recipients.

claim: Redirection of MHC class II-restricted thymocytes to the CD8-lineage in OT-II RB3 mice is cell-intrinsic.
source: As expected, B6.SJL thymocytes and OT-II cells developed normally, while OT-II RB3 thymocytes developed into mature CD8SP cells (Figure 1F), demonstrating that redirection of MHC class II-restricted thymocytes to the CD8-lineage in OT-II RB3 mice is cell-intrinsic and could not be compensated by the presence of WT B6.SJL cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and stated in the text, based on mixed bone marrow chimera experiments.

claim: Redirection of MHC class II-restricted thymocytes to the CD8-lineage in OT-II RB3 mice could not be compensated by the presence of WT B6.SJL cells.
source: As expected, B6.SJL thymocytes and OT-II cells developed normally, while OT-II RB3 thymocytes developed into mature CD8SP cells (Figure 1F), demonstrating that redirection of MHC class II-restricted thymocytes to the CD8-lineage in OT-II RB3 mice is cell-intrinsic and could not be compensated by the presence of WT B6.SJL cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and stated in the text.

claim: ThPOK promotes CD4-lineage commitment.
source: CD4/CD8-lineage choice is determined by the careful coordination between the lineage-determining transcription factors ThPOK and Runx3, where ThPOK promotes CD4-lineage commitment and Runx3 promotes CD8-lineage commitment (Dave et al., 1998; Woolf et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Dave et al., 1998 and Woolf et al., 2003.

claim: Runx3 promotes CD8-lineage commitment.
source: CD4/CD8-lineage choice is determined by the careful coordination between the lineage-determining transcription factors ThPOK and Runx3, where ThPOK promotes CD4-lineage commitment and Runx3 promotes CD8-lineage commitment (Dave et al., 1998; Woolf et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Dave et al., 1998 and Woolf et al., 2003.

claim: ThPOK and Runx3 antagonize each other's expression.
source: These transcription factors antagonize each other's expression, while promoting the expression of CD4 or CD8-lineage genes (Sakaguchi et al., 2015; Luckey et al., 2014; Egawa and Littman, 2008; Wildt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: ThPOK and Runx3 promote the expression of CD4 or CD8-lineage genes, respectively.
source: These transcription factors antagonize each other's expression, while promoting the expression of CD4 or CD8-lineage genes (Sakaguchi et al., 2015; Luckey et al., 2014; Egawa and Littman, 2008; Wildt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple sources.

claim: MHC class I-restricted OT-I-expressing thymocytes decreased CD8α during Phase 1 and re-expressed CD8α during Phase 2.
source: As shown previously (Kimura et al., 2016), MHC class I-restricted OT-I-expressing thymocytes decreased CD8α during Phase 1 and re-expressed CD8α during Phase 2, coinciding with CD8-lineage commitment (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and cited from Kimura et al., 2016.

claim: Runx3 was induced during Phase 2 in OT-I thymocytes.
source: In addition, Runx3 was induced during Phase 2 (Figure 2B), demonstrating that Runx3 is expressed when cells commit to the CD8-lineage.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Runx3 is expressed when cells commit to the CD8-lineage.
source: In addition, Runx3 was induced during Phase 2 (Figure 2B), demonstrating that Runx3 is expressed when cells commit to the CD8-lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of Runx3 expression in OT-I thymocytes.

claim: OT-II and OT-II RB thymocytes exhibited a consistent decrease in CD8α expression through Phases 1–2.
source: OT-II and OT-II RB thymocytes exhibited a consistent decrease in CD8α expression through Phases 1–2 and no expression of Runx3 (Figure 2B), as expected for MHC class II-restricted thymocytes that commit to the CD4-lineage.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OT-II and OT-II RB thymocytes showed no expression of Runx3.
source: OT-II and OT-II RB thymocytes exhibited a consistent decrease in CD8α expression through Phases 1–2 and no expression of Runx3 (Figure 2B), as expected for MHC class II-restricted thymocytes that commit to the CD4-lineage.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OT-II RB3 mice showed premature expression of Runx3 during Phase 1 of lineage choice.
source: However, OT-II RB3 mice showed premature expression of Runx3 during Phase 1 of lineage choice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion of HDAC3 leads to an acceleration of commitment to the CD8-lineage.
source: Therefore, deletion of HDAC3 leads to an acceleration of commitment to the CD8-lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the premature expression of Runx3 and high CD8α expression during Phase 1 in OT-II RB3 mice.

claim: ThPOK is induced in phase 1 in MHC class II-restricted thymocytes.
source: As expected, ThPOK was induced during Phase one in OT-II and OT-II RB mice and maintained at high levels in Phase 2, while in OT-I mice, ThPOK was expressed at low levels during Phase one but repressed at Phase 2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ThPOK was expressed at low levels during Phase one but repressed at Phase 2 in OT-I mice.
source: As expected, ThPOK was induced during Phase one in OT-II and OT-II RB mice and maintained at high levels in Phase 2, while in OT-I mice, ThPOK was expressed at low levels during Phase one but repressed at Phase 2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The downregulation of ThPOK at Phase two in OT-I mice corresponded with the induction of Runx3 at Phase 2.
source: The downregulation of ThPOK at Phase two in OT-I mice corresponded with the induction of Runx3 at Phase 2 (Figure 2B–C), illustrating antagonism between Runx3 and ThPOK during lineage commitment.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2B-C.

claim: OT-II RB3 mice failed to induce ThPOK expression during Phase 1.
source: On the other hand, OT-II RB3 mice failed to induce ThPOK expression during Phase 1 (Figure 2C), which coincided with premature expression of Runx3 at this phase (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 64% of CD4-lineage genes were significantly down-regulated in HDAC3-deficient Selecting cells.
source: 64% of CD4-lineage genes in this gene set were significantly down-regulated in HDAC3-deficient cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and stated in the text.

claim: 53% of CD8-lineage genes were significantly up-regulated in OT-II HDAC3-cKO cells compared to OT-II.
source: However, 53% of CD8-lineage genes were significantly up-regulated in OT-II HDAC3-cKO cells compared to OT-II (Figure 3D), such as Snai3, Cd8a, Cd8b1, Prf1, Itgae, Gpr114, and Runx3 (Figure 3—figure supplements 2C and 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and stated in the text.

claim: There was a decrease in ThPOK expression at the Selecting (CD69+) stage in OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice compared to OT-II mice.
source: Protein expression showed a similar pattern, as there was a decrease in ThPOK expression and slight increase in Runx3 expression at the Selecting (CD69+) stage in OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice compared to OT-II mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There was a slight increase in Runx3 expression at the Selecting (CD69+) stage in OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice compared to OT-II mice.
source: Protein expression showed a similar pattern, as there was a decrease in ThPOK expression and slight increase in Runx3 expression at the Selecting (CD69+) stage in OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice compared to OT-II mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Lack of HDAC3 leads to a gene expression pattern predisposed to the CD8-lineage and against the CD4-lineage prior to positive selection.
source: This distinct pattern suggests that lack of HDAC3 leads to a gene expression pattern predisposed to the CD8-lineage and against the CD4-lineage prior to positive selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing down-regulation of CD4-lineage genes and up-regulation of CD8-lineage genes.

claim: There was a significant increase in the average H3K27ac signal around the TSS of CD8-lineage genes in OT-II HDAC3-cKO Selecting cells compared to OT-II.
source: However, there was a significant increase in the average H3K27ac signal and average H3K9ac signal around the TSS of CD8-lineage genes (e.g. Cd8a, Cd8b1, Snai3, Runx3, Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: HDAC3-deficient thymocytes induce CD8-lineage genes and fail to prompt the CD4-lineage program after receiving a TCR signal.
source: Altogether, this shows that HDAC3-deficient thymocytes induce CD8-lineage genes and fail to prompt the CD4-lineage program after receiving a TCR signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Super-enhancers are areas of the genome that control genes important for cell type specification.
source: Super-enhancers are areas of the genome that control genes important for cell type specification (Hnisz et al., 2013; Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hnisz et al., 2013 and Whyte et al., 2013.

claim: Very high levels of H3K27ac reliably characterize super-enhancers.
source: Very high levels of H3K27ac reliably characterize super-enhancers (Hnisz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hnisz et al., 2013.

claim: Deletion of HDAC3 leads to an increase in the number of enhancers in Immature (DP) cells.
source: Using the ROSE (Rank Ordering of Super-Enhancers) algorithm to identify super-enhancers (Whyte et al., 2013; Lovén et al., 2013) within the Immature (DP) compartment, 5967 typical-enhancers were identified from OT-II mice and 7496 typical enhancers from OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice, while 263 super-enhancers were identified from OT-II mice and 360 super-enhancers from OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice (Figure 4A), demonstrating that deletion of HDAC3 leads to an increase in the number of enhancers.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and stated in the text.

claim: There was a significant increase in H3K27ac signal at super-enhancers from HDAC3-deficient cells compared to WT.
source: Further examination revealed a significant increase in H3K27ac signal at super-enhancers from HDAC3-deficient cells compared to WT (Figure 4B–C), while the average H3K27ac signal at typical enhancers remained largely unchanged (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4B-C.

claim: The median length of super-enhancers was increased in HDAC3-cKO cells compared to OT-II mice.
source: Not only was the H3K27ac signal increased at super enhancers in HDAC3-cKO cells but the median length was also increased compared to the OT-II mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in acetylation at super-enhancers from OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice corresponded to an increase in gene expression of genes associated with super-enhancers.
source: In addition, the increase in acetylation at super-enhancers from OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice corresponded to an increase in gene expression of genes associated with super-enhancers, compared to OT-II mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 197 super-enhancers overlapped between OT-II and OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice.
source: 197 super-enhancers overlapped between the two mice, 66 super-enhancers were unique to OT-II mice, and 163 super-enhancers were unique to OT-II HDAC3-cKO mice (Figure 4F).

claim: 66 super-enhancers were unique to OT-II mice.
